newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Killers apologise for death of U.S. student.
newsitem.headline: Killers apologise for death of U.S. student.

text.p: Four black youths who were part of a mob that killed a white U.S. student in a South African township apologised to her parents on Tuesday but said they had acted out of political conviction.

The four, who are serving 18-year prison terms for the 1993 murder of Amy Biehl in Guguletu township outside Cape Town, issued the apologies during a public application for amnesty to Archbishop Desmond Tutu's Truth and Reconciliation Commission.

Biehl's parents, Peter and Linda, had flown to South Africa from California to attend the hearings. They have said they do not oppose the amnesty applications, which are part of South Africa's attempts to heal the wounds of the apartheid race war.
One of the four, Vusumzi Ntamo, acknowledged in a statement to the commission that he was mentally backward and described himself as someone who followed others.
"I think I do suffer from some mental incapacity," he said. "I am not able to properly articulate any political ideology or motivation for my conduct."

In their statements the four, all now in their early 20s, described chasing Biehl down a Guguletu street after her car was stopped by a crowd of youths who had attended a meeting of the radical Pan Africanist Congress (PAC).
Mongezi Manqina told the commission he had tripped Biehl and and delivered what he believed was the fatal knife wound while she lay on the ground. Other youths rained rocks on her body.
"At the time we were in high spirits...We had no mercy on white people," another of the four youths, Ntobeko Peni, said.
He said he had realised later that Biehl was trying to help South Africa's blacks and he regretted having taken part in killing her.
"I realise it was bad," he said. "I ask Amy's parents to forgive me. Just to hear they have forgiven me would mean a great deal to me."
Biehl's parents, who are due to address the hearing later on Tuesday, shook hands at the start of proceedings with family and friends of the four youths.
The four said in their statements that they were influenced by the PAC slogan "one settler, one bullet", and understood this to mean that all whites should be killed.
"Killing every white person meant the land would come back to the African people," Peni said.

The Truth Commission was set up in 1995 to investigate human rights abuses by all sides during more than four decades of apartheid. It has powers to grant amnesty to perpetrators who make full confessions.

At the time Biehl was murdered, South Africa was in the final stages of preparing for all-race elections in April 1994 that marked the final end of apartheid. The PAC won less than two percent of the vote.
